# Self-report

*To be written by the student: how the work proceeded, what was difficult,
time-consuming or fun, what was relatively easy, collaboration and sources
used (including AI tools).*

\newpage

```{r data}
A  <- as.matrix(read.table("data/A.txt"))   # forward operator (n x n)
dimnames(A) <- NULL
d0 <- scan("data/seis00.txt", quiet = TRUE)
d1 <- scan("data/seis01.txt", quiet = TRUE)
d2 <- scan("data/seis02.txt", quiet = TRUE)
n  <- nrow(A)
z  <- 1:n
```

```{r functions}
# Prior covariance: exponential correlation function
exp_cov <- function(n, sigma2, ell) {
  D <- abs(outer(1:n, 1:n, "-"))           # matrix of |i - j|
  sigma2 * exp(-3 * D / ell)
}

# Posterior of m | d for d = A m + eps (Gaussian conditioning)
gauss_posterior <- function(d, A, mu, Sigma, sigma2_eps) {
  Sigma_d <- A %*% Sigma %*% t(A) + sigma2_eps * diag(nrow(A))   # Cov(d)
  K       <- Sigma %*% t(A) %*% solve(Sigma_d)                   # Cov(m,d) Cov(d)^-1
  mu_post <- drop(mu + K %*% (d - A %*% mu))
  S_post  <- Sigma - K %*% A %*% Sigma
  S_post  <- (S_post + t(S_post)) / 2      # make exactly symmetric (rounding)
  list(mean = mu_post, cov = S_post)
}

# Simulate B draws from N(mu, S): m = mu + L x, L L^T = S, x ~ N(0, I)
rmvn <- function(B, mu, S) {
  L <- t(chol(S + 1e-10 * diag(length(mu))))   # lower Cholesky factor (tiny jitter)
  X <- matrix(rnorm(length(mu) * B), length(mu), B)
  t(mu + L %*% X)                               # one draw per row
}

# Mean with pointwise 95% credibility band (and optional realisations)
band_plot <- function(mean, sd, main, ylim, sims = NULL) {
  lo <- mean - 1.96 * sd
  hi <- mean + 1.96 * sd
  plot(z, mean, type = "n", ylim = ylim, xlab = "Index i", ylab = "m_i", main = main)
  polygon(c(z, rev(z)), c(lo, rev(hi)), col = "grey85", border = NA)
  if (!is.null(sims)) matlines(z, t(sims), lty = 1, lwd = 1,
                               col = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3", "#e7298a", "#66a61e"))
  lines(z, mean, lwd = 2)
}
```

# Part 1

## 1a)

Since $\vm$ and $\bm\varepsilon$ are independent and Gaussian, $(\vm,\vd)$ is a linear
transformation of a Gaussian vector and therefore jointly Gaussian, with
\begin{align*}
E(\vd) &= \vA\bm\mu_m,\\
\operatorname{Cov}(\vd) &= \vA\bm\Sigma_m\vA^\top+\sigma_\varepsilon^2\vI \;=:\; \bm\Sigma_d,\\
\operatorname{Cov}(\vd,\vm) &= \operatorname{Cov}(\vA\vm+\bm\varepsilon,\vm)=\vA\bm\Sigma_m,
\end{align*}
so
$$
\begin{pmatrix}\vm\\ \vd\end{pmatrix}\sim N\!\left(
\begin{pmatrix}\bm\mu_m\\ \vA\bm\mu_m\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}\bm\Sigma_m & \bm\Sigma_m\vA^\top\\
\vA\bm\Sigma_m & \bm\Sigma_d\end{pmatrix}\right).
$$
The conditional distribution of a partitioned Gaussian gives the posterior
$\vm\mid\vd\sim N(\bm\mu_{m\mid d},\bm\Sigma_{m\mid d})$ with
\begin{align*}
\bm\mu_{m\mid d} &= \bm\mu_m+\bm\Sigma_m\vA^\top\bm\Sigma_d^{-1}(\vd-\vA\bm\mu_m),\\
\bm\Sigma_{m\mid d} &= \bm\Sigma_m-\bm\Sigma_m\vA^\top\bm\Sigma_d^{-1}\vA\bm\Sigma_m .
\end{align*}
The pointwise 95% credibility interval for $m_i$ is
$(\bm\mu_{m\mid d})_i\pm1.96\sqrt{(\bm\Sigma_{m\mid d})_{ii}}$.

## 1b)

```{r prior, fig.cap="Prior expectation (black), 95\\% credibility interval (grey) and five simulated profiles."}
mu <- 0; sigma2_m <- 1; ell <- 20; sigma2_eps <- 0.04
mu_m    <- rep(mu, n)
Sigma_m <- exp_cov(n, sigma2_m, ell)

set.seed(1)
prior_sims <- rmvn(5, mu_m, Sigma_m)
band_plot(mu_m, sqrt(diag(Sigma_m)), "Prior", ylim = c(-3.5, 3.5), sims = prior_sims)
```

Since $\Sigma_{m,ii}=1$, the prior is $m_i\sim N(0,1)$ and the interval is $0\pm1.96$ for
all $i$. The profiles are simulated as $\bm\mu_m+\mathbf L\bm x$, with
$\mathbf L\mathbf L^\top=\bm\Sigma_m$ (Cholesky) and $\bm x\sim N(\mathbf 0,\vI)$.

## 1c)

```{r post00, fig.cap="Posterior expectation (black) and 95\\% credibility interval (grey) given seis00. Dashed: prior interval."}
post0 <- gauss_posterior(d0, A, mu_m, Sigma_m, sigma2_eps)
sd0   <- sqrt(diag(post0$cov))
band_plot(post0$mean, sd0, "Posterior given seis00", ylim = c(-3.5, 3.5))
abline(h = c(-1.96, 1.96), lty = 2, col = "grey40")
```

```{r covimages, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Prior (left) and posterior (right) covariance matrices, same colour scale."}
cov_image <- function(S, main, zlim) {
  image(z, z, t(S)[, n:1], zlim = zlim, col = hcl.colors(64, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE),
        xlab = "j", ylab = "i", main = main, axes = FALSE, useRaster = TRUE)
  axis(1); axis(2, at = n + 1 - c(1, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100), labels = c(1, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100))
  box()
}
zl <- range(Sigma_m, post0$cov)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
cov_image(Sigma_m, "Prior covariance", zl)
cov_image(post0$cov, "Posterior covariance", zl)
```

```{r postnumbers}
sd_range <- range(sd0)
A_one    <- max(abs(A %*% rep(1, n)))      # A applied to a constant vector
```

The posterior standard deviations are `r round(sd_range[1], 2)`--`r round(sd_range[2], 2)`,
compared with 1 in the prior. The uncertainty is reduced, but much remains, and the
posterior covariance is spread further from the diagonal. One reason is that
$\vA\mathbf 1=\mathbf 0$ (the rows of $\vA$ sum to zero). The data therefore
contain no information about the overall level of $\vm$, only about local changes.

## 1d)

```{r exceedance}
c_lev <- -1
h_V   <- function(m, c = c_lev) sum((c - m) * (m < c))   # exceedance volume

B <- 100
set.seed(2)
post_sims <- rmvn(B, post0$mean, post0$cov)
V <- apply(post_sims, 1, h_V)                              # one V per posterior draw

V_summary <- c(mean = mean(V), median = median(V), sd = sd(V))
knitr::kable(t(round(V_summary, 2)), caption = "Posterior summaries of $V$ ($B=100$).")
```

```{r Vhist, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="Histogram of 100 posterior samples of $V$."}
hist(V, breaks = 20, col = "grey80", border = "white", main = "", xlab = "V")
```

We draw $\vm^{(b)}\sim N(\bm\mu_{m\mid d},\bm\Sigma_{m\mid d})$, $b=1,\dots,100$, and compute
$V^{(b)}=h(\vm^{(b)})$. The posterior of $V$ is right-skewed, so the mean is larger
than the median.

## 1e)

```{r percentiles}
Vs  <- sort(V)                                      # order statistics
P10 <- Vs[10]
P90 <- Vs[90]

# N = number of samples below the true P10 ~ Bin(B, 0.1)
# V_(r) <= P10 < V_(s)  <=>  r <= N <= s - 1
r <- qbinom(0.025, B, 0.1)
s <- qbinom(0.975, B, 0.1) + 1
coverage <- pbinom(s - 1, B, 0.1) - pbinom(r - 1, B, 0.1)
```

Estimates from the ordered samples: $\widehat P_{10}=V_{(10)}=`r round(P10, 2)`$ and
$\widehat P_{90}=V_{(90)}=`r round(P90, 2)`$.

The number of samples below $P_{10}$ is $N\sim\mathrm{Bin}(100,0.1)$. Since
$V_{(r)}\le P_{10}<V_{(s)}$ exactly when $r\le N\le s-1$,
$$
P\big(V_{(r)}\le P_{10}<V_{(s)}\big)=\sum_{k=r}^{s-1}\binom{100}{k}0.1^k0.9^{100-k}.
$$
With $r=`r r`$ and $s=`r s`$ this probability is `r round(coverage, 3)`, which gives
the interval $[V_{(`r r`)},V_{(`r s`)}]=[`r round(Vs[r], 2)`,\ `r round(Vs[s], 2)`]$ for
$P_{10}$. The interval is wide compared with the estimate, so $B=100$ is not
sufficient for a precise $P_{10}$, and $B$ should be increased.

## 1f)

```{r permtest, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="Lag-1 correlation for 1000 permutations of seis00 (histogram) and for the observed data (red line)."}
lag1 <- function(x) cor(x[-1], x[-length(x)])   # lag-1 correlation

rho_obs <- lag1(d0)
set.seed(4)
rho_perm <- replicate(1000, lag1(sample(d0)))    # sample() gives a random permutation
n_extreme <- sum(abs(rho_perm) >= abs(rho_obs))

hist(rho_perm, breaks = 30, col = "grey80", border = "white", main = "",
     xlab = "Lag-1 correlation", xlim = c(-0.4, 1))
abline(v = rho_obs, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

If the data were exchangeable, the observed order would be as likely as any
permutation, and $\hat\rho_1$ would look like the permuted values. The observed
lag-1 correlation is $\hat\rho_1=`r round(rho_obs, 2)`$, while the permuted values lie in
$[`r round(min(rho_perm), 2)`,\ `r round(max(rho_perm), 2)`]$.
`r if (n_extreme == 0) "None" else n_extreme` of the 1000 permutations are as extreme
($p<0.001$), so the claim of exchangeability is rejected. Neighbouring samples are
strongly correlated, as expected from $\vd=\vA\vm+\bm\varepsilon$.

# Part 2

## 2a)

For a given $(T,B)$ only the prior mean changes, to $\bm\mu_m^{T,B}$; the covariance
is as in Part 1. From 1a, the marginal distribution of the data is
$$
p(\vd\mid T,B)=N\big(\vd;\ \vA\bm\mu_m^{T,B},\ \bm\Sigma_d\big),\qquad
\bm\Sigma_d=\vA\bm\Sigma_m\vA^\top+\sigma_\varepsilon^2\vI ,
$$
and Bayes' rule gives, for $(T,B)\in\mathcal G$,
$$
p(T,B\mid\vd)=\frac{p(\vd\mid T,B)\,p(T,B)}{\sum_{(T',B')\in\mathcal G}p(\vd\mid T',B')\,p(T',B')}
\;\propto\;\exp\!\Big\{-\tfrac12(\vd-\vA\bm\mu_m^{T,B})^\top\bm\Sigma_d^{-1}(\vd-\vA\bm\mu_m^{T,B})\Big\},
$$
since the prior $p(T,B)=1/|\mathcal G|$ and the normalising constant of the Gaussian
do not depend on $(T,B)$. Here $|\mathcal G|=751$ pairs.

```{r p2setup}
dmu <- 5
G   <- subset(expand.grid(T = 30:60, B = 40:70), T <= B)    # admissible (T, B)
G$dZ <- G$B - G$T + 1                                       # thickness

# Prior mean for a zone from T to B (T = NA: no zone)
mu_TB <- function(T, B) {
  m <- rep(mu, n)
  if (!is.na(T)) m[T:B] <- mu - dmu
  m
}

Sigma_d <- A %*% Sigma_m %*% t(A) + sigma2_eps * diag(n)
L_d     <- t(chol(Sigma_d))                                 # Sigma_d = L_d L_d^T

# log p(d | mean) up to a constant common to all models
loglik <- function(d, mean_m) {
  r <- forwardsolve(L_d, d - A %*% mean_m)                  # L_d^-1 (d - A mu)
  -0.5 * sum(r^2)
}

log_sum_exp <- function(x) max(x) + log(sum(exp(x - max(x))))

zone_posterior <- function(d) {
  ll <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(G)), function(k) loglik(d, mu_TB(G$T[k], G$B[k])))
  list(ll = ll, post = exp(ll - log_sum_exp(ll)))           # uniform prior cancels
}

zp1 <- zone_posterior(d1)
zp2 <- zone_posterior(d2)
```

```{r heatmaps, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Joint posterior $p(T,B\\mid\\mathbf d)$ for seis01 (left) and seis02 (right). Grey: inadmissible pairs."}
heat <- function(post, main) {
  M <- matrix(NA, 31, 31, dimnames = list(30:60, 40:70))
  M[cbind(G$T - 29, G$B - 39)] <- post
  image(30:60, 40:70, M, col = hcl.colors(64, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE),
        xlab = "Top T", ylab = "Base B", main = main)
  image(30:60, 40:70, ifelse(is.na(M), 1, NA), col = "grey85", add = TRUE)
  box()
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
heat(zp1$post, "seis01")
heat(zp2$post, "seis02")
```

```{r priormarg, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=2.4, fig.cap="Marginal prior of top $T$, base $B$ and thickness $\\Delta Z$ (uniform prior on $\\mathcal G$)."}
marg <- function(w, v, levels) sapply(levels, function(x) sum(w[v == x]))
prior_G <- rep(1 / nrow(G), nrow(G))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(30:60, marg(prior_G, G$T,  30:60), type = "h", lwd = 3, xlab = "Top T",  ylab = "Prior prob.")
plot(40:70, marg(prior_G, G$B,  40:70), type = "h", lwd = 3, xlab = "Base B", ylab = "Prior prob.")
plot(1:41,  marg(prior_G, G$dZ, 1:41),  type = "h", lwd = 3, xlab = "Thickness dZ", ylab = "Prior prob.")
```

```{r postmarg, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="Marginal posterior of $T$, $B$ and $\\Delta Z$. Top row: seis01, bottom row: seis02."}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
for (zp in list(zp1, zp2)) {
  plot(30:60, marg(zp$post, G$T,  30:60), type = "h", lwd = 3, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Top T",  ylab = "Posterior prob.")
  plot(40:70, marg(zp$post, G$B,  40:70), type = "h", lwd = 3, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Base B", ylab = "Posterior prob.")
  plot(1:41,  marg(zp$post, G$dZ, 1:41),  type = "h", lwd = 3, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Thickness dZ", ylab = "Posterior prob.")
}
```

```{r p2summary}
summ <- function(post) {
  k <- which.max(post)
  c(T = G$T[k], B = G$B[k], dZ = G$dZ[k], prob = post[k], E_dZ = sum(post * G$dZ))
}
tab2a <- rbind(seis01 = summ(zp1$post), seis02 = summ(zp2$post))
knitr::kable(tab2a, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 3, 2),
             col.names = c("T", "B", "dZ", "posterior prob.", "E(dZ | d)"),
             caption = "Posterior mode of $(T,B)$, its probability, and posterior mean thickness.")
```

The uniform prior on $\mathcal G$ does not give uniform marginals, because the
number of admissible partners varies. $T$ is uniform up to 40 and then decreasing,
$B$ is increasing up to 50 and then uniform, and $\Delta Z$ is most likely around
11 and least likely for very thick zones. The data overrule this completely. The posterior is concentrated on almost a single pair: a zone
from `r tab2a[1, "T"]` to `r tab2a[1, "B"]` ($\Delta Z=`r tab2a[1, "dZ"]`$) for seis01,
and from `r tab2a[2, "T"]` to `r tab2a[2, "B"]` ($\Delta Z=`r tab2a[2, "dZ"]`$) for
seis02. The remaining uncertainty is at most one sample in $T$ or $B$. A shift of
$\Delta\mu=5$ is large compared with $\sigma_m=1$ and gives strong reflections at the top
and base of the zone, so they are easy to locate.

## 2b)

The no-zone case is a single model ($\bm\mu_m=\mu\mathbf 1$, as in Part 1), while the zone
case consists of $|\mathcal G|=`r nrow(G)`$ models. Giving every one of the
$`r nrow(G) + 1`$ models the same prior probability would give $P(\text{no zone})=1/`r nrow(G) + 1`$.
That would say we are almost certain a zone exists, only because there are many
ways to place it. The prior probability of the zero case should instead express
our belief about whether a zone is present at all, and the remaining probability
should then be spread over $\mathcal G$. We use
$$
P(\text{no zone})=\tfrac12,\qquad p(T,B)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal G|},\ (T,B)\in\mathcal G .
$$
Then
$$
P(\text{no zone}\mid\vd)=\frac{\tfrac12\,p(\vd\mid\text{no zone})}
{\tfrac12\,p(\vd\mid\text{no zone})+\tfrac12\,\frac1{|\mathcal G|}\sum_{\mathcal G}p(\vd\mid T,B)} .
$$

```{r p2b}
p0 <- 1 / 2
post_zero <- function(zp, d) {
  l0 <- log(p0)     + loglik(d, mu_TB(NA, NA))
  lz <- log(1 - p0) + log_sum_exp(zp$ll) - log(nrow(G))
  exp(l0 - log_sum_exp(c(l0, lz)))
}
pz <- c(seis01 = post_zero(zp1, d1), seis02 = post_zero(zp2, d2))
```

The posterior probability of zero thickness is `r signif(pz[1], 2)` for seis01 and
`r signif(pz[2], 2)` for seis02. The data are so much more likely under the zone
models that both data sets clearly indicate a zone. Any reasonable choice of
$P(\text{no zone})$ gives the same conclusion.

## 2c)

Let the action be $a_1$ (invest) or $a_0$ (do not invest), with loss equal to minus the
profit:
$$
L(a_1,V)=-(aV-b),\qquad L(a_0,V)=0 .
$$
The Bayes decision minimises the posterior expected loss:
$E\{L(a_1,V)\mid\vd\}=-(aE(V\mid\vd)-b)$ and $E\{L(a_0,V)\mid\vd\}=0$. Hence
$$
\text{invest}\iff E(V\mid\vd)>\frac ba = 10 .
$$
$V$ is the exceedance volume from 1d. Its posterior combines the uncertainty in the
zone and in $\vm$:
$p(V\mid\vd)=\sum_{\text{models}}P(\text{model}\mid\vd)\,p(V\mid\vd,\text{model})$. We
simulate a model (no zone or $(T,B)$) from its posterior (2b), and then
$\vm\mid\vd,T,B\sim N(\bm\mu_{m\mid d}^{T,B},\bm\Sigma_{m\mid d})$ from 1a with prior mean
$\bm\mu_m^{T,B}$, and compute $V=h(\vm)$.

```{r p2c}
a <- 1; b <- 10; B_mc <- 5000
K_gain <- Sigma_m %*% t(A) %*% solve(Sigma_d)
L_post <- t(chol(post0$cov + 1e-10 * diag(n)))             # same posterior covariance as 1c

sim_V <- function(zp, d, pz0) {
  w   <- c(pz0, (1 - pz0) * zp$post)                       # no zone + all (T, B)
  Tm  <- c(NA, G$T); Bm <- c(NA, G$B)
  idx <- sample(length(w), B_mc, replace = TRUE, prob = w)
  sapply(idx, function(k) {
    mu_k <- mu_TB(Tm[k], Bm[k])
    m    <- mu_k + K_gain %*% (d - A %*% mu_k) + L_post %*% rnorm(n)
    h_V(m)
  })
}
set.seed(5)
V1 <- sim_V(zp1, d1, pz[1])
V2 <- sim_V(zp2, d2, pz[2])
profit <- list(seis01 = a * V1 - b, seis02 = a * V2 - b)

tab2c <- t(sapply(profit, function(x)
  c(EV = mean(x + b) / a, E_profit = mean(x), P_loss = mean(x < 0),
    P10 = unname(quantile(x, 0.1)), P50 = median(x), P90 = unname(quantile(x, 0.9)))))
knitr::kable(tab2c, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("E(V|d)", "E(profit|d)", "P(profit<0|d)", "P10", "P50", "P90"),
             caption = "Posterior summaries of $V$ and the profit $aV-b$ (5000 simulations).")
```

```{r profithist, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Posterior distribution of the profit $V-10$. Red line: break-even."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (nm in names(profit)) {
  hist(profit[[nm]], breaks = 30, col = "grey80", border = "white", main = nm,
       xlab = "Profit", xlim = range(-5, profit[[nm]]))
  abline(v = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}
```

**Recommendation.** For both data sets $E(V\mid\vd)$ is far above $b/a=10$, so the
recommendation is to invest in both cases. None of the 5000 simulations gives a loss in either case
($P(\text{profit}<0\mid\vd)<1/5000$).
The expected profit is much larger for seis02 (thicker zone). To the decision
makers I would present the uncertainty as the profit distribution (histograms above) with
$P_{10}$, $P_{50}$, $P_{90}$ and the probability of a loss, rather than a single number.

If $V$ is instead read as the thickness $\Delta Z$, the rule becomes
$E(\Delta Z\mid\vd)>10$. This gives
$E(\Delta Z\mid\vd)=`r round(tab2a[1, "E_dZ"], 1)`$ (do not invest) for seis01 and
`r round(tab2a[2, "E_dZ"], 1)` (invest) for seis02.

# Part 3

## 3a)

Write $\vm=\mu\mathbf 1-\Delta\mu\,\mathbf 1_{[T,B]}+\bm x$ with $\bm x\sim N(\mathbf 0,\bm\Sigma_m)$
independent of $\mu\sim N(\mu_0,\tau_\mu^2)$. By double expectation and total variance,
\begin{align*}
E(\vm) &= E\{E(\vm\mid\mu)\}=\mu_0\mathbf 1-\Delta\mu\,\mathbf 1_{[T,B]},\\
\operatorname{Cov}(\vm) &= E\{\operatorname{Cov}(\vm\mid\mu)\}+\operatorname{Cov}\{E(\vm\mid\mu)\}
=\bm\Sigma_m+\tau_\mu^2\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top ,
\end{align*}
and therefore
$$
E(\vd)=\vA E(\vm),\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\vd)=\vA\bm\Sigma_m\vA^\top+\tau_\mu^2(\vA\mathbf 1)(\vA\mathbf 1)^\top+\sigma_\varepsilon^2\vI .
$$
With $\mu_0=0$ the mean is unchanged. Since the rows of $\vA$ sum to zero,
$\vA\mathbf 1=\mathbf 0$, so the extra term vanishes and $\operatorname{Cov}(\vd)$ is also
unchanged. Hence $p(\vd\mid T,B)$, and so $p(T,B\mid\vd)$, are exactly the same as in 2a.

```{r p3a}
tau2_mu <- 0.25
Sigma_m_mu <- Sigma_m + tau2_mu * matrix(1, n, n)            # Cov(m) with uncertain mu
Sigma_d_mu <- A %*% Sigma_m_mu %*% t(A) + sigma2_eps * diag(n)
L_d_save <- L_d
L_d <- t(chol(Sigma_d_mu))                                    # loglik() now uses new Cov(d)
zp1_mu <- zone_posterior(d1)
L_d <- L_d_save                                               # restore
diff3a <- c(cov_d = max(abs(Sigma_d_mu - Sigma_d)), post = max(abs(zp1_mu$post - zp1$post)))
```

Numerically, for seis01, the largest change in $\operatorname{Cov}(\vd)$ is
`r signif(diff3a["cov_d"], 2)` and the largest change in $p(T,B\mid\vd)$ is
`r signif(diff3a["post"], 2)` (rounding error). The result is not surprising. The
data only see changes in $\vm$ (1c), so uncertainty about a common level
cannot affect the inference about $T$ and $B$. It only adds uncertainty about the
absolute level of $\vm$.

## 3b)

With $\sigma_\varepsilon^2=\nu\sigma_m^2$ and $\mathbf R=\bm\Sigma_m/\sigma_m^2$ (the correlation
matrix), $\operatorname{Cov}(\vd)=\sigma_m^2\mathbf C$ with $\mathbf C=\vA\mathbf R\vA^\top+\nu\vI$, so
for a given $(T,B)$
$$
p(\vd\mid\sigma_m^2,T,B)\propto(\sigma_m^2)^{-n/2}\exp\Big\{-\frac{Q_{T,B}}{2\sigma_m^2}\Big\},\qquad
Q_{T,B}=(\vd-\vA\bm\mu_m^{T,B})^\top\mathbf C^{-1}(\vd-\vA\bm\mu_m^{T,B}).
$$
The conjugate prior is $\sigma_m^2\sim\mathrm{IG}(\alpha,\beta)$, and then
$$
p(\sigma_m^2\mid\vd,T,B)\propto(\sigma_m^2)^{-(\alpha+n/2)-1}\exp\Big\{-\frac{\beta+Q_{T,B}/2}{\sigma_m^2}\Big\}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\sigma_m^2\mid\vd,T,B\sim\mathrm{IG}\big(\alpha+\tfrac n2,\ \beta+\tfrac12Q_{T,B}\big).
$$
Since $(T,B)$ is unknown,
$p(\sigma_m^2\mid\vd)=\sum_{\mathcal G}p(T,B\mid\vd)\,\mathrm{IG}(\sigma_m^2;\alpha+\frac n2,\beta+\frac12Q_{T,B})$,
with $p(T,B\mid\vd)$ from 3c. We use $\alpha=2,\ \beta=1$ (prior mean 1, the value used
so far, and heavy tails) and $\nu=0.04$, so $\mathbf C$ is the same matrix as $\bm\Sigma_d$ in Part 2.

```{r p3b}
alpha <- 2; beta <- 1; nu <- 0.04
C_mat <- A %*% (Sigma_m / sigma2_m) %*% t(A) + nu * diag(n)
L_C   <- t(chol(C_mat))
Q_TB  <- function(d) sapply(seq_len(nrow(G)), function(k) {
  r <- forwardsolve(L_C, d - A %*% mu_TB(G$T[k], G$B[k]))
  sum(r^2)
})

# 3c: p(T,B | d) with sigma_m^2 integrated out (Student-t marginal likelihood)
zone_posterior_t <- function(Q) {
  lw <- -(alpha + n / 2) * log(beta + Q / 2)
  exp(lw - log_sum_exp(lw))
}
Q1 <- Q_TB(d1); Q2 <- Q_TB(d2)
pt1 <- zone_posterior_t(Q1); pt2 <- zone_posterior_t(Q2)

# Posterior of sigma_m^2: mixture of inverse-gammas, summarised by simulation
sim_sigma2 <- function(Q, w, N = 20000) {
  k <- sample(length(w), N, replace = TRUE, prob = w)
  1 / rgamma(N, shape = alpha + n / 2, rate = beta + Q[k] / 2)
}
set.seed(6)
s2_1 <- sim_sigma2(Q1, pt1); s2_2 <- sim_sigma2(Q2, pt2)
tab3b <- rbind(seis01 = c(mean(s2_1), quantile(s2_1, c(0.025, 0.975))),
               seis02 = c(mean(s2_2), quantile(s2_2, c(0.025, 0.975))))
knitr::kable(tab3b, digits = 2, col.names = c("posterior mean", "2.5%", "97.5%"),
             caption = "Posterior mean and 95\\% credibility interval for $\\sigma_m^2$.")
```

```{r p3bplot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="Prior IG(2,1) (grey) and posterior densities of $\\sigma_m^2$ for seis01 and seis02."}
dinvgamma <- function(x, a, b) exp(a * log(b) - lgamma(a) - (a + 1) * log(x) - b / x)
mix_dens  <- function(x, Q, w) sapply(x, function(s)
  sum(w * dinvgamma(s, alpha + n / 2, beta + Q / 2)))
xs <- seq(0.05, 2.5, length.out = 400)
plot(xs, mix_dens(xs, Q1, pt1), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#1b9e77",
     xlab = expression(sigma[m]^2), ylab = "Density",
     ylim = c(0, max(mix_dens(xs, Q2, pt2), mix_dens(xs, Q1, pt1))))
lines(xs, mix_dens(xs, Q2, pt2), lwd = 2, col = "#d95f02")
lines(xs, dinvgamma(xs, alpha, beta), lwd = 2, col = "grey60")
legend("topright", c("prior", "seis01", "seis02"), lwd = 2,
       col = c("grey60", "#1b9e77", "#d95f02"), bty = "n")
```

The posterior is much narrower than the prior. For seis01 it is centred somewhat
above the value $\sigma_m^2=1$ that was assumed in Parts 1--2, and for seis02 close to it.

## 3c)

The variance uncertainty is accounted for by integrating $\sigma_m^2$ out of the
likelihood instead of fixing it:
$$
p(\vd\mid T,B)=\int p(\vd\mid\sigma_m^2,T,B)\,p(\sigma_m^2)\,d\sigma_m^2
\;\propto\;\Big(\beta+\tfrac12Q_{T,B}\Big)^{-(\alpha+n/2)},
$$
which is a multivariate Student-$t$ density with $2\alpha$ degrees of freedom. The
factor $|\mathbf C|^{-1/2}$ and the gamma-function constants are the same for all
$(T,B)$. With the uniform prior on $\mathcal G$,
$p(T,B\mid\vd)\propto(\beta+\frac12Q_{T,B})^{-(\alpha+n/2)}$. For fixed $\sigma_m^2=1$ it was
$\propto\exp(-\frac12Q_{T,B})$.

```{r p3c}
cmp <- function(pf, pt) {
  kf <- which.max(pf); kt <- which.max(pt)
  c(mode_fixed = paste0("(", G$T[kf], ",", G$B[kf], ")"), prob_fixed = round(pf[kf], 3),
    E_dZ_fixed = round(sum(pf * G$dZ), 2),
    mode_t = paste0("(", G$T[kt], ",", G$B[kt], ")"), prob_t = round(pt[kt], 3),
    E_dZ_t = round(sum(pt * G$dZ), 2))
}
tab3c <- rbind(seis01 = cmp(zp1$post, pt1), seis02 = cmp(zp2$post, pt2))
knitr::kable(tab3c, col.names = c("mode", "prob.", "E(dZ|d)", "mode", "prob.", "E(dZ|d)"),
             caption = "Posterior of $(T,B)$ with fixed $\\sigma_m^2=1$ (columns 1--3) and with $\\sigma_m^2$ integrated out (columns 4--6).")
```

The most probable pair is unchanged. With $\sigma_m^2$ integrated out, the posterior is
slightly less concentrated: the probability of the mode falls from
`r tab3c[1, "prob_fixed"]` to `r tab3c[1, "prob_t"]` for seis01, and from
`r tab3c[2, "prob_fixed"]` to `r tab3c[2, "prob_t"]` for seis02. The reason is that the
data suggest a scale at or above 1 (3b). A larger scale makes the neighbouring
pairs relatively more plausible, and the heavier Student-$t$ tails also allow more
spread. The effect is largest for seis01, where $E(\sigma_m^2\mid\vd)$ is furthest from 1.
The conclusions from Part 2 do not change.
